# Introduction{-}
In _absorption spectroscopy_, light with a specific frequency is sent through a material that we wish to analyse. Depending on the composition of the material, light will be absorbed more at some frequencies compared to others. For instance, @fig-plot shows the spectra of two different sugar compounds.
The absorption in a mix depends on the concentration of the individual materials, the frequency of the light, and the distance the lights travels through the material.^[The Lambert-Beer law is a physical model stating that the absorption is proportional to the concentration, the path length through the material, and a molar attenuation coefficient.]

Within _spectral unmixing_, the goal is to determine the individual concentrations of chemical components based on the spectrum of a mixture of materials with known spectra.
Based on the measurements in @fig-plot, one could for instance imagine determining the concentration of the two compounds in an unknown sugar mixture.

![An example of spectral measurements of two different sugar compounds. The plot is generated from two different datasets ([Beta-D-lactose](https://ramanbase.org/spectra/135293), [D-ribose](https://ramanbase.org/spectra/134366)) from Raman Base^[Raman Base: Open online database of Raman Spectra. Institute of Scientific Instruments of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Brno, Czech Republic. Accessible at [https://ramanbase.org/](https://ramanbase.org/)] published under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) with a non-commercial restriction.](plotEN.svg){#fig-plot width=90% fig-alt="Raman spectra for two different sugar compounds."}

We imagine that we have performed $n$ experiments with (that is, sent light through) a mixture of $m$ materials in various solutions and at $p$ frequencies. The results of the experiment are collected in an $n\times p$-matrix $D$, where each row represents an absorption experiment using the chosen frequencies. Our goal is to determine the individual concentrations of the $m$ materials.

The process can be described by two real matrices $C$ and $S$. $C$ is an $n\times m$-matrix containing the unknown concentrations in such a way that each column corresponds to a material, and each row corresponds to an experiment with a certain solution of materials.
$S$, on the other hand, is a known $p\times m$-matrix with so-called _pure component spectra_, containing coefficients of proportionality at specific frequencies. That means that we have measured the potential components (think of lactose and ribose as in @fig-plot) separately and know the absorption at different frequencies.
These frequencies are chosen such that there is only a single component that is strongly absorbent &ndash; in @fig-plot, lactose is for instance seen to have a strong peak around 350, while ribose has one around 550. The idea is to use this to determine the concentrations in the unknown solution.

In total, the measurements are given by an $n\times p$-matrix
$$D=CS^\top.$$
From this, it is seen that $DS=CS^\top\! S$. If the matrix $S^\top\! S$ is invertible, then we can utilize this to determine $C$ from $D$ and $S$ since
$$C = DS(S^\top\! S)^{-1}$${#eq-CSolve}
in this case.
Therefore, we analyse when $S^\top\! S$ is invertible. In practice, one would have measurement errors on $D$, which makes the estimation of $C$ more cumbersome than in @eq-CSolve. Here, however, we ignore such measurement errors to make the computations doable by hand.

:::{.callout-note title="Note"}
In mathematics, _spectrum_ is sometimes used to describe the set of eigenvalues of a matrix. This is not the same meaning of _spectrum_ as used in spectroscopy like in this workshop.
:::

# Exericse 1{#sec-opg1}
In this exercise, we consider a toy example with specific matrices $D$ and $S$. To make the computations easier to perform by hand, the matrices do not come from an actual spectroscopy measurement. Let
$$D=\left[
    \begin{array}{rrr}
      2 & 1 & -4\\
      2 & 3 &  0\\
      6 & 1 &  2\\
      4 & 0 & -6
    \end{array}
  \right]
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  S=\left[
    \begin{array}{rrr}
      2 &  2 &  0\\
      1 & -1 &  2\\
      2 & -2 & -2
    \end{array}\right].$$


1. Show by direct calculation that the matrix $S^\top\! S$ is given by
$$S^\top\! S=\left[
      \begin{array}{rrr}
         9 & -1 & -2\\
        -1 &  9 &  2\\
        -2 &  2 &  8
      \end{array}
    \right].$$
  

1. Show that $\mathbf{v}_1=[1,\, -1,\, 2]^\top$ and $\mathbf{v}_2=[1,\, -1,\,-1]^\top$ are eigenvectors of $S^\top\! S$. What are the corresponding eigenvalues?
  
1. It turns out that the characteristic polynomial for $S^\top\! S$ is given by
$$-(\lambda-12)(\lambda-8)(\lambda-6).$$

   Use this information to determine the remaining eigenvalue of $S^\top\! S$, and determine the (why can there by only one?) corresponding eigenvector.

1. Utilize the results from 2 and 3 to write out a diagonalization for $S^\top\! S$.

1. Use the diagonalization from above to find the inverse matrix $(S^\top\! S)^{-1}$. Afterwards, determine $C$ via @eq-CSolve.

# Exercise 2{#sec-opg2}
We now consider in greater generality when $S^\top\! S$ is invertible.

1. Explain that a vector $\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}$ is in the null space of $S^\top\! S$ if and only if $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector for $S^\top {S}$ with eigenvalue $0$.

   Argue that when such an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ exists, it must be the case that $\dim\mathrm{Null}(S^\top\! S)\geq 1$.

1. Use the observation above to argue that $S^\top\! S$ has full rank if and only if all of its eigenvalues are non-zero.

   :::{.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse=true}
   Use the rank-nullity theorem.
   :::

1. Recall that $S$ is a $p\times m$-matrix. Can $S^\top\! S$ be invertible if $m>p$?

   :::{.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse=true}
   If $S\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$, we also have $S^\top\! S\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. Is it then possible for $S^\top\! S$ have full rank if $S$ is _not_ of full rank?
   :::

# Exercise 3{#sec-opg3}
In this exercise, we analyse the inverse of $S^\top\! S$ using diagonalization. We will apply a theorem which ensures that any real, symmetric matrix is diagonalizable.

1. Show that $S^\top\! S$ is symmetric and conclude from the comment above that there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that
$$S^\top\! S = PDP^{-1}.$$
   What are the diagonal entries in $D$, and what are the columns of $P$?

1. Show that the determinant of $S^\top\! S$ is given by the eigenvalues of the matrix via the formula
$$\det(S^\top\! S) = \prod_{i = 1}^m \lambda_i = \lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots \lambda_m.$$
   Does this agree with item 2 of @sec-opg2?

   :::{.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse=true}
   Use the diagonalization of $S^\top\! S$ as well as the multiplicative property of the determinant.
   :::

1. Now, assume that $S^\top\! S$ is invertible. Show that the inverse is given by
$$(S^\top\! S)^{-1} = PD^{-1}P^{-1}$$
Additionally, express $D^{-1}$ in terms of $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_m$.
